'''Rick L. Danheiser''' is an American [[Organic chemistry|organic]] chemist and is the [[Arthur C. Cope]] Professor of Chemistry at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] and chair of the MIT faculty.  His research involves the invention of new methods for the synthesis of complex organic compounds. Danheiser is known for the [[Danheiser annulation]] and [[Danheiser benzannulation]] reactions.

== Education ==
Danheiser was born in New York and received his B.A. in 1972 at [[Columbia College (New York)|Columbia College]].<ref name="MIT-Rick-bio">Danheiser, Rick L. "[http://chemistry.mit.edu/people/danheiser-rick Rick Lane Danheiser] A C Cope Professor of Chemistry." Chemistry Directory. MIT, Web. 23 Nov. 2014.</ref> While working as an undergraduate under the direction of [[Gilbert Stork]], Danheiser developed a method for the regiospecific alkylation of beta-diketone enol ethers (the "Stork-Danheiser Alkylation").<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stork |first1=G. |last2=Danheiser |first2=R. L. |title=The Regiospecific Alkylation of Cyclic b Diketone Enol Ethers. A General Synthesis of 2-Alkylcyclohexenones |journal=J. Org. Chem. |date=1973 |volume=38 |issue=9 |pages=1775–1776 |doi=10.1021/jo00949a048 }}</ref> and employed it in a [[total synthesis]] of the spiro sesquiterpene beta-vetivone.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stork |first1=G. |last2=Danheiser |first2=R. L. |last3=Ganem |first3=B. |title=Spiroannelation of Enol Ethers of Cyclic 1,3-Diketones. A Simple Stereospecific Synthesis of -Vetivone |journal=J. Am. Chem. Soc. |date=1973 |volume=95 |issue=10 |pages=3414–3415 |doi=10.1021/ja00791a074 }}</ref>  Danheiser received his Ph.D. at [[Harvard University]] in 1978.  His doctoral research (under the direction of [[E. J. Corey]]) involved the first total synthesis of the diterpene plant growth hormone [[gibberellic acid]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Corey |first1=E. J. |last2=Danheiser |first2=R. L. |last3=Chandrasekaran |first3=S. |last4=Siret |first4=P. |last5=Keck |first5=G. E. |last6=Gras |first6=J.-L. |title=Stereospecific Total Synthesis of Gibberellic Acid. A Key Tricyclic Intermediate |journal=J. Am. Chem. Soc.|date=1978 |volume=100 |issue=25 |page=8031 |doi=10.1021/ja00493a055 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Corey |first1=E. J. |last2=Danheiser |first2=R. L. |last3=Chandrasekaran |first3=S. |last4=Keck |first4=G. E. |last5=Gopalan |first5=B. |last6=Larsen |first6=S. D. |last7=Siret |first7=P. |last8=Gras |first8=J.-L. |title=Stereospecific Total Synthesis of Gibberellic Acid |journal=J. Am. Chem. Soc. |date=1978 |volume=100 |issue=25 |page=8034 |doi=10.1021/ja00493a055 }}</ref><ref>Jandh. "[http://academictree.org/chemistry/peopleinfo.php?pid=56102 Rick L. Danheiser Details]." Chemistry Tree, 11 Dec. 2011. Web. 23 Nov. 2014.</ref>

== Research ==
Danheiser's research has focused on the development of new strategies for the synthesis of complex molecules and their application in the total synthesis of natural products.  Synthetic methods invented in his laboratory include highly stereoselective [4 + 1] cyclopentene annulations based on oxyanion and carbanion-accelerated vinylcyclopropane rearrangements;<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Danheiser |first1=R. L. |last2=Bronson |first2=J. J. |last3=Okano |first3=K. |title=The Carbanion-Accelerated Vinylcyclopropane Rearrangement. Application in a General, Stereocontrolled Annulation Approach to Cyclopentene Derivatives |journal=J. Am. Chem. Soc. |date=1985 |volume=107 |issue=15 |page=4579 |doi=10.1021/ja00301a051 }}</ref> the application of organosilanes (e.g., allenylsilanes, propargylsilanes, and allylsilanes) in a general [3 + 2] annulation strategy for the synthesis of five-membered carbocycles and heterocycles (the "Danheiser Annulation");<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Danheiser |first1=R. L. |last2=Carini |first2=D. J. |last3=Basak |first3=A. |title=TMS-Cyclopentene Annulation: A Regiocontrolled Approach to the Synthesis of Five-Membered Rings |journal=J. Am. Chem. Soc. |date=1981 |volume=103 |issue=6 |page=1604 |doi=10.1021/ja00301a051 |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00396a071|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Kurti |first1=L. |last2=Czako |first2=B. |title=Strategic Applications of Named Reactions in Organic Synthesis |date=2005 |publisher=Elsevier Academic Press |isbn=0-12-429785-4 |pages=124–125}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Li |first1=J. J. |title=Name Reactions |date=2002 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |isbn=3-540-43024-5 |page=90}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Hassner |first1=A. |last2=Namboothiri |first2=I. |title=Name Reactions |date=2012 |publisher=Elsevier Academic Press |isbn=978-0-08-096630-4 |page=112}}</ref> benzannulation strategies based on pericyclic transformations of vinylketenes (“[[Danheiser benzannulation]]”);<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Danheiser |first1=R. L. |last2=Gee |first2=S. K. |title=A Regiocontrolled Annulation Approach to Highly Substituted Aromatic Compounds |journal=J. Org. Chem. |date=1984 |volume=49 |issue=9 |page=1672 |doi=10.1021/jo00183a043}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Kurti |first1=L. |last2=Czako |first2=B. |title=Strategic Applications of Named Reactions in Organic Synthesis |date=2005 |publisher=Elsevier Academic Press |isbn=0-12-429785-4 |pages=122–124}}</ref> methods for the synthesis of aromatic and dihydroaromatic compounds based on cycloadditions of highly unsaturated conjugated molecules such as conjugated 1,3-enynes;<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Danheiser |first1=R. L. |last2=Gould |first2=A. E. |last3=Fernandez de la Pradilla |first3=R. |last4=Helgason |first4=A. L. |title=Intramolecular [4 + 2] Cycloaddition Reactions of Conjugated Enynes |journal=J. Org. Chem. |date=1994 |volume=59 |issue=19 |page=5514 |doi=10.1021/jo00098a002 }}</ref> and formal [2 + 2 + 2] cycloadditions based on propargylic ene reaction/Diels-Alder cycloaddition cascades.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sakai |first1=T. |last2=Danheiser |first2=R. L. |title=Cyano Diels-Alder and Cyano Ene Reactions. Applications in a Formal [2 + 2 +2] Cycloaddition Strategy for the Synthesis of Pyridines |journal=J. Am. Chem. Soc. |date=2010 |volume=132 |issue=38 |pages=13203–13205 |doi=10.1021/ja106901u |pmid=20815385 |pmc=2944912 }}</ref>  Natural products synthesized in his laboratory at MIT include the neurotoxic alkaloids anatoxin a<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Danheiser |first1=R. L. |last2=Morin |first2=J. M. |last3=Salaski |first3=E. J. |title=An Efficient Total Synthesis of Anatoxin a |journal=J. Am. Chem. Soc. |date=1985 |volume=107 |issue=26 |page=8066 |doi=10.1021/ja00312a045 }}</ref> and quinolizidine 217A,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Maloney |first1=K. M. |last2=Danheiser |first2=R. L. |title=Total Synthesis Quinolizidine Alkaloid (-)-217A. Application of Iminoacetonitrile Cycloadditions in Organic Synthesis |journal=Org. Lett. |date=2005 |volume=7 |issue=14 |pages=3115–3118 |doi=10.1021/ol051185n |pmid=15987219 |pmc=3203637 }}</ref> the immunosuppressant agent mycophenolic acid<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Danheiser |first1=R. L. |last2=Gee |first2=S. K. |last3=Perez |first3=J. J. |title=The Total Synthesis of Mycophenolic Acid |journal=J. Am. Chem. Soc. |date=1986 |volume=108 |issue=4 |page=806 |doi=10.1021/ja00264a038 }}</ref> the antitumor agent ascochlorin<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dudley |first1=G. B. |last2=Takaki |first2=K. S. |last3=Cha |first3=D. D. |last4=Danheiser |first4=R. L. |title=Total Synthesis of (-)-Ascochlorin via a Cyclobutenone-Based Benzannulation Strategy |journal=Org. Lett. |date=2000 |volume=2 |issue=21 |pages=3407–10 |doi=10.1021/ol006561c |pmid=11029223 |url=https://figshare.com/articles/Total_Synthesis_of_-Ascochlorin_via_a_Cyclobutenone-Based_Benzannulation_Strategy/3737322 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> and a number of diterpene quinones derived from the Chinese traditional medicine ''Dan Shen''.

== Notable research awards ==
Danheiser was awarded the Cope Scholar Award of the [[American Chemical Society]] in 1995.<ref>{{cite web |title=Arthur C. Cope Scholar Awards |url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/arthur-cope-scholar-award.html |website=American Chemical Society |accessdate=19 March 2019}}</ref> He is a Fellow of the American Chemical Society.<ref>{{cite web |title=2017 ACS Fellows |url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/fellows/list-of-2017-acs-fellows.html#P179_13145 |website=American Chemical Society |accessdate=19 March 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=ACS National Award Winners |journal=Chem. Eng. News |date=1994 |volume=72 |issue=46 |pages=49–54 |doi=10.1021/cen-v072n046.p049 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Teaching and service ==
Danheiser has a particular interest in reproducibility in scientific research.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bergman |first1=R. G. |last2=Danheiser |first2=R. L. |title=Reproducibility in Chemical Research |journal=Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. |date=2016 |volume=55 |issue=41 |pages=12548–12549 |doi=10.1002/anie.201606591|pmid=27558212 |url=https://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/1721.1/114628/1/ACIE%202016%2055%20xxx.pdf |hdl=1721.1/114628 |doi-access=free }}</ref>  He has been the editor-in-chief of the journal ''[[Organic Syntheses]]'' and a member of the board of directors of the Organic Syntheses corporation since 2004. Organic Syntheses has the unusual feature that all data and experiments reported in articles must be confirmed in the laboratory of a member of the editorial board prior to publication.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Danheiser |first1=R. L. |title=Organic Syntheses: The 'Gold Standard' in Experimental Synthetic Organic Chemistry |journal=Org. Synth. |date=2011 |volume=88 |pages=1–3 |doi=10.15227/orgsyn.088.0001|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Danheiser has a longstanding interest in laboratory safety and at MIT he has served as the chair of several committees including the MIT Chemistry Department EHS Committee which was recognized in 1991 as the first recipient of the American Chemical Society Division of Chemical Safety national award for "best university safety program".<ref>{{cite web |title=SafetyStratus College and University Health and Safety Award |url=http://dchas.org/chas-award-nominations/college-and-university-health-and-safety-award/ |website=ACS Division of Chemical Health and Safety |accessdate=19 March 2019}}</ref>{{failed verification|date=July 2019}} Danheiser also served on the National Research Council Committee on Prudent Practices for the Handling, Storage and Disposal of Chemicals in Laboratories, chairing the Subcommittee on Assessing Chemical Hazards.<ref>{{cite book |title=Prudent Practices in the Laboratory: Handling and Disposal of Chemicals |date=1995 |publisher=National Academies Press |isbn=978-0-309-21158-1 |url=https://www.nap.edu/read/4911/chapter/1|doi=10.17226/4911 }}</ref>

At MIT, Danheiser's educational contributions have been recognized with a MacVicar Faculty Fellowship,<ref>{{cite web |title=MIT Names 3 MacVicar Fellows, Recognizing Outstanding Teaching |url=https://news.mit.edu/1996/macvicars |website=MIT News |date=2 February 1996 |accessdate=19 March 2019}}</ref> the School of Science Prize for Excellence in Undergraduate Teaching,<ref>{{cite web |title=Teaching prize recipients |url=https://science.mit.edu/about/awards/science-teaching-prizes/teaching-prize-recipients/#undergraduate |website=MIT School of Science |accessdate=19 March 2019 |archive-date=30 July 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190730094646/https://science.mit.edu/about/awards/science-teaching-prizes/teaching-prize-recipients/#undergraduate |url-status=dead }}</ref> the MIT Graduate Student Council Teaching Award, and the School of Science Prize for Graduate Education.<ref>{{cite web |title=School of Science announces winners of Teaching Prizes for Graduate and Undergraduate Education |url=https://science.mit.edu/school-of-science-announces-winners-of-teaching-prizes-for-graduate-and-undergraduate-education/ |website=MIT School of Science |accessdate=19 March 2019}}</ref>
